AWS SDK
AWS Software Development Kits
Call AWS from your code, without hardcoded keys.
Libraries (Python, JavaScript, Java, etc.) that let an application call the AWS APIs. They sign requests and retrieve credentials through a standard provider chain.
Saves you from writing request signing and API request handling by hand.
The credential chain lets you use an IAM role with no key in the code.
Handles retries and pagination, so applications are more reliable.
Code that uses an execution role stays compliant with least privilege.
The SDK looks for credentials in order: environment variables, profiles/SSO, then the container or instance role (metadata). It then signs each API call.
A Lambda function reads an S3 object with its execution role.
An application on EC2 sends SQS messages.
A Python security audit script goes through the accounts.
A mobile application uses temporary credentials via Cognito.
Never write the access key and secret key in the code or the repository: use a role or a managed secret.

AWS CloudShell
A terminal in the browser, already authenticated.
Free shell launched from the AWS console, with the CLI preinstalled and your session's credentials. It avoids storing access keys on a local machine.
No access keys to create or keep on your computer.
Inherits the permissions of the signed-in identity: least privilege applies.
Ready-to-use environment with the CLI and common tools.
Access can be controlled or denied by an IAM policy.
In the console, you open CloudShell. A temporary environment starts with your session's credentials, and persistent storage is available in your home directory.
Run a quick CLI command with no local setup.
Work from a shared or untrusted machine.
Test an audit script before automating it.
Troubleshoot a resource during an incident.
For long tasks or pipelines, use a dedicated automation environment, not an interactive shell.

AWS CDK
AWS Cloud Development Kit
Infrastructure as real code: Python, TypeScript, Java...
Framework that lets you define AWS infrastructure in a programming language, then synthesize it into CloudFormation templates deployed through stacks.
High-level constructs apply good defaults (encryption, least privilege).
Infrastructure is reviewed, tested and versioned like code.
Tools like cdk-nag check security rules before deployment.
Reduces duplication: a secure construct is reused everywhere.
You write the CDK app, the cdk synth command generates the CloudFormation template, then cdk deploy deploys it. A prior bootstrap creates the necessary roles and resources in the account.
Create a VPC, an encrypted bucket and IAM roles through code.
Standardize an architecture across multiple accounts.
Integrate infrastructure tests into a pipeline.
Generate resources in a loop when a YAML template becomes unwieldy.
If the team prefers purely declarative, plain CloudFormation is enough; the CDK adds a layer to understand.

AWS X-Ray
Follow a request across all the services of an application.
Distributed tracing service: it follows requests end to end through an application, builds a service map and helps spot errors and latency. Useful for understanding the path of a request.
Locates the slow or failing service in an architecture with several components.
The service map helps you understand dependencies and data flows.
Provides context during an incident investigation on an application.
Tracing must avoid capturing sensitive data in annotations.
The instrumented application sends trace segments to X-Ray; the service assembles them into traces and a service map. An IAM role must allow the data to be sent.
Find out why an API Gateway + Lambda is slow.
Visualize dependencies between microservices.
Spot a failing call from one service.
Correlate an error spike with a specific component.
For new instrumentation, AWS increasingly points to OpenTelemetry; X-Ray remains the trace backend.

CloudWatch monitors metrics and logs; X-Ray follows the path of a request.

AWS Well-Architected
AWS Well-Architected Framework / Tool
A framework of best practices for evaluating an architecture.

AWS framework described in six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost optimization, sustainability) with an assessment tool (Well-Architected Tool) that produces recommendations.
Gives a common language to review an architecture and prioritize risks.
The Security pillar covers identity, detection, data protection and incident response.
The tool identifies high risks and proposes an improvement plan.
Lenses cover specific cases (for example serverless, SaaS).
You answer questions per pillar in the Well-Architected Tool; it flags risks and suggests actions. Reviews are redone regularly.
Review an architecture before going to production.
Prepare an internal security audit.
Compare two designs against the six pillars.
Structure an architecture discussion with the team.
It is neither a technical scanner nor a detection service: it provides a review framework, not continuous monitoring.

Trusted Advisor is automatic and technical; Well-Architected is a review guided by questions.

Security principles: traceability, security at all layers, data protection, automation.
AWS FIS
AWS Fault Injection Service
Cause controlled failures to test resilience.
Chaos engineering service: it injects controlled failures (instance shutdown, network latency, API errors) through experiments to verify that an application holds up.
Reveals resilience weaknesses before a real incident exposes them.
Stop conditions (CloudWatch alarms) halt the experiment if the impact becomes too strong.
The experiment runs with an IAM role limited to the intended targets.
Validates that alarms, runbooks and failover work.
You define an experiment template: actions, target resources, stop conditions and an IAM role. The run applies the actions, and the team observes how the system reacts.
Check that the application survives the loss of an instance.
Simulate an AZ failure in pre-production.
Test alarms and automatic failover.
Train the team on a failure scenario.
No testing in a fragile environment or without stop conditions; start with a small scope in pre-production.

AWS Resilience Hub
Measure whether an application meets its RTO and RPO objectives.
Service that assesses an application's resilience against a resilience policy (RTO and RPO objectives), provides recommendations and tracks compliance over time.
Translates business objectives (RTO/RPO) into technical checks.
Detects single points of failure in the architecture.
Provides concrete recommendations to close the gaps.
Integrates with FIS to test failure scenarios.

You describe the application (resources via CloudFormation, resource groups, etc.), define a resilience policy, then run an assessment that compares the architecture with the objectives and recommends fixes.
Check that an application meets a 1-hour RTO.
Validate a disaster recovery architecture.

OpenTelemetry
OpenTelemetry (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry)
The open standard for producing traces, metrics and logs.
Open, vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting applications and collecting traces, metrics and logs. AWS provides a distribution (ADOT) that sends this data to X-Ray, CloudWatch or Prometheus.
Avoids lock-in: the same instrumentation works with several observability tools.
The collector can filter or mask sensitive attributes before sending.
Gives consistent traces across multi-service applications.
AWS increasingly recommends it for instrumentation, notably with X-Ray.
Code or an agent produces telemetry data; an OpenTelemetry collector receives it, processes it, then exports it to a backend such as X-Ray, CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus.
Instrument an application in a vendor-neutral way.
Send traces to X-Ray with the ADOT collector.
Mask sensitive data in telemetry.
Unify metrics, logs and traces from several services.
It is an instrumentation standard, not a storage backend or a threat detection tool.

AWS CodeBuild
Compile and test in a disposable, isolated environment.
Managed build service: it compiles code, runs tests and produces artifacts in ephemeral containers, with no build server to administer. The steps are described in a buildspec file.
Each build runs in an isolated, ephemeral environment.
A service role limits what the build can do (least privilege).
Secrets come from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not from code.
Can run security analyses (SAST, dependency scanning) in the pipeline.
CodeBuild reads buildspec.yml, starts a container, runs the phases (install, build, post_build), publishes the artifacts (for example to S3) and sends the logs to CloudWatch or S3.

AWS CodeDeploy
Deploy automatically, with rollback if something breaks.
Automated deployment service for EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda and ECS. It manages strategies (in-place, blue/green) and can automatically roll back on failure.
Repeatable deployments: fewer human errors and direct changes in production.
Blue/green deployment limits downtime and risk.
Automatic rollback if the deployment fails or an alarm fires.
An IAM service role and instance profile limit what the deployment can do.
An appspec file describes the steps; on EC2 or on-premises, a CodeDeploy agent retrieves the revision (S3 or GitHub) and installs it. For Lambda and ECS, traffic is shifted between versions.

AWS CodePipeline
The CI/CD chain: source, build, test, approval, deployment.
Continuous integration and delivery service that orchestrates stages (source, build, test, deployment) and can include manual approvals. It connects CodeBuild, CodeDeploy and other services.
Automates the chain: fewer manual deployments and untraced changes.
Manual approvals enforce human control before production.
Each stage uses distinct IAM roles, which makes separation of duties easier.
Artifacts stored in S3, encrypted with KMS.
A trigger (Git push, EventBridge event) starts the pipeline: each stage runs actions and passes its artifacts to the next. A service role authorizes the actions.
